newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US, Russia sign follow-on accords on START-1.
newsitem.headline: US, Russia sign follow-on accords on START-1.

text.p: U.S. and Russian arms officials, joined by counterparts from Belarus, Kazakhstan and the Ukraine, on Tuesday signed accords to improve the implementation of the 1991 Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, a U.S. statement said.
It gave no details of the secret joint statements and agreement reached in five-week-long negotiations by the treaty's Joint Compliance and Inspection Commission.

But a U.S. official familiar with the negotiations in Geneva said that most of the documents signed by the five states party to START-1 would reduce the extent of installations and other sensitive sites to be inspected.
"Eleven of the 13 documents had to do with reducing the facilities," he said.
He also said that Russia and the United States were ahead of schedule in reducing their strategic nuclear offensive arms under START-1, signed by Presidents Bush and Gorbachev in 1991.
The cooperation should establish a "good basis" for eventually implementing the long-stalled START-2, which the Russian Duma (parliament) has yet to ratify, he added.

The START-1 treaty, which went into effect in December 1994, aims to reduce the long-range nuclear forces of Washington and Moscow by 30-40 per cent. It provides for inspection of 120-130 sites, including about 33 in America, the U.S. official said.

"Another really good accomplishment here is that both the Russian Federation and the U.S. are ahead of schedule in the reductions under the START-1 treaty. Quite a few hundred of warheads, missiles and silos are being removed and eliminated," the U.S. official said.
"We are ahead of the game," he added, referring to the first three-year deadline for eliminations which is set for December. "This is proceeding more than apace.
"Both militaries, as part of downsizing, are proceeding faster with these eliminations."

In November, Belarus -- the last former Soviet state outside Russia which still had missiles on its soil -- sent its last Soviet-era nuclear warheads for destruction in Russia. The Ukraine handed them over earlier in 1996 and Belarus in 1995.

The deadline for removing them was set at the end of 1996 under the 1992 Lisbon protocol, which settled with Washington the fate of missiles left outside Russia when the Soviet Union broke up in 1991.
"They had a lot of the strategic offensive weapons spread over that whole, huge Soviet Union from Kazakhstan to Belarus," the U.S. official said.
"We are continuing very actively to conduct inspections of all three countries even though warheads have been eliminated. The facilities have not been eliminated," he added.
The Joint Commission is expected to hold a fresh round of talks in October, according to the U.S. official.
